section_summary: This section comprises U.S. State Department correspondence, diplomatic telegrams, and War Department intelligence reports from January through April 1941 concerning political tensions and economic strains in Japan. Key records document the domestic controversy and structural curtailment of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association (Taisei Yokusankai), the reorganization of the Konoye Cabinet with business and military leaders like Masatsune Ogura, Teijiro Toyoda, and Teiichi Suzuki, and back-channel efforts by Home Minister Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma to restrain Army radicals. The section also covers reporting on Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka's mission to Berlin, Rome, and Moscow, as well as detailed military attaché career summaries for newly appointed Japanese generals.

subfiles.about: Transmits to the American Ambassador in Tokyo a copy of a memorandum of conversation on the internal situation in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State transmits Instruction No. 211 to American Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo. The instruction encloses for confidential information a copy of a memorandum of conversation held on January 14, 1941, between Reverend George S. Noss and an officer of the Department. The enclosed discussion pertains to internal political, social, and economic developments in Japan.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 211 to the American Ambassador at Tokyo

subfiles.about: Records observations by a returned American missionary regarding economic distress, food shortages, public disillusionment, and war sentiment in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Reverend George S. Noss, a Reformed Church missionary who lived in northern Japan for over twenty years, reports severe food shortages, transportation breakdowns, and widespread mis-employment affecting 20 to 25 percent of workers. He notes that the Japanese public is completely disillusioned with the China incident and that government propaganda regarding the southward advance has had little effect. Despite economic deterioration, Noss observes no likelihood of a social revolution and believes that with the military in firm control, war between Japan and the United States is inevitable. He also discusses looming severe police restrictions on foreign Christian missionaries and offers his personal services to the State Department.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation: Japanese Internal Situation

subfiles.about: Analyzes Japanese diplomatic methods and concludes that threats and press bluster by Matsuoka represent bluffing to intimidate the United States.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck recalls an anecdote concerning Henry W. Denison, an American adviser to the Japanese Foreign Office before the Russo-Japanese War, who advised drafting a conciliatory note once war had been decided upon, demonstrating that responsible Japanese statesmen do not bluster prior to attacking. He argues that Foreign Minister Matsuoka and the Japanese press are engaging in intimidation at German behest to diminish American aid to Britain, foster isolationism, and paralyze U.S. policy in the Far East. Hornbeck emphasizes that Japan is unprepared for war with the United States and that Matsuoka's aggressive rhetoric is a bluff that should not be taken at face value.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Stanley K. Hornbeck on Japanese Threats and U.S. Policy

subfiles.about: Reports on political unrest, impending Cabinet reorganization, economic distress, and Diet opposition to the Imperial Rule Assistance Association.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports mounting indications of a Cabinet reorganization driven by criticism of Prime Minister Konoye and public discontent over commodity controls. Living conditions for the general population and civil servants are declining into squalor, with widespread food shortages and black markets demonstrating breakdowns in official regimentation. Public alarm and Diet resistance have emerged against the totalitarian ambitions of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association, prompting plans for its reorganization. Grew suggests that Konoye may relinquish the premiership to focus on the IRAA, potentially being succeeded by Baron Hiranuma as a moderating influence against extremists. He concludes that internal difficulties and American defense preparations are leading Japanese leaders toward increased caution.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 390 (Sections 1–5) from Tokyo regarding Cabinet Crisis and the IRAA

subfiles.about: Transmits a Japanese-language newspaper clipping concerning Premier Konoye's Taisei Yokusankai to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Seunghak Cho of War Department G-2 writes to the State Department enclosing a Japanese newspaper clipping concerning the Taisei Yokusankai (Imperial Rule Assistance Association) headed by Premier Konoye. Cho highlights the association as one of the most powerful organizations in Japan and suggests the material may be useful as intelligence. He offers to provide an English translation if desired by the Department.
subfiles.title: Letter from Seunghak Cho transmitting Japanese Newspaper Clipping

subfiles.about: Reports Diet proceedings and ministerial statements regarding the budget, legal status, and reorganization of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association.
subfiles.summary: This Japanese newspaper clipping reports on Diet proceedings regarding the Taisei Yokusankai (Imperial Rule Assistance Association). Premier Fumimaro Konoye and key ministers prepare unified replies to Diet interpellations concerning the nature, budget, and constitutional position of the association, clarifying that it is an auxiliary public organ rather than a political party or dictatorship. It details discussions on domestic politics, civil rights under the Peace Preservation Police Law, and relations with the Imperial Diet. The clipping also includes contemporary advertisements and notices from an overseas Japanese-language publication.
subfiles.title: Japanese Newspaper Clipping regarding Diet Debate on the Taisei Yokusankai

subfiles.about: Summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 5402 analyzing attacks on and the impending reorganization of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association.
subfiles.summary: Herbert M. Fales summarizes Ambassador Grew's Despatch No. 5402 regarding the present status and significance of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association (IRAA). The memorandum details how the IRAA was vigorously attacked both in and out of the Diet as unconstitutional, fascist, communist, cumbersome, and faulty in personnel. It notes that Diet approval of an 8 million yen appropriation was accompanied by demands for structural and personnel reorganization, concluding that the association is unlikely to become the nucleus of a totalitarian state.
subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 5402

subfiles.about: Provides a detailed analysis of Diet opposition, ideological criticism, and the planned reorganization of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew provides a comprehensive account of parliamentary debates and public criticism regarding the Imperial Rule Assistance Association. Opponents led by former party figures, including Katsu Kawasaki and Yukio Ozaki, assailed the IRAA as unconstitutional, authoritarian, and an illegitimate usurpation of parliamentary functions. To preserve national harmony, the Konoye government compromised by reducing the association's annual budget from 100 million to 8 million yen and pledging a thorough reorganization to strip it of policymaking authority. Grew concludes that while former party leaders did not destroy the association, their resistance prevented the IRAA from becoming a dominant totalitarian party controlling the state.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5402 from Tokyo: The Present Status and Significance of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association

subfiles.about: Outlines four coordinated totalitarian movements in Japan and details Foreign Minister Matsuoka's European diplomatic mission.
subfiles.summary: Seunghak Cho submits intelligence based on Japanese-language press reports describing four major Japanese nationalist organizations working toward totalitarian goals: Taisei Yokusankai, Greater Asia League, Asia Promotion Association (Koa Dan), and Japan Pacific Institute. Cho reports that the Taisei Yokusankai enjoys Army backing and is designed to merge all political parties into a single fascist structure. He also notes that Foreign Minister Matsuoka's journey to Berlin and Rome involves operational military and economic commissions between the Tripartite Pact signatories.
subfiles.title: Letter from Seunghak Cho on Japanese Political Movements and Matsuoka's Trip

subfiles.about: Reports the resignation of Count Arima and IRAA officials and the expected appointment of Justice Minister Yanagawa as Vice President.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that Tokyo newspapers announce the resignation of Count Yoriyasu Arima, Secretary-General of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association, along with forty other officials. Approximately 450 association employees met to discuss an en bloc resignation, although collective action was deferred. Minister of Justice Lieutenant General Heisuke Yanagawa is expected to assume the vice presidency of the association concurrently with a Cabinet post without portfolio, foreshadowing a complete organizational overhaul.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 472 from Tokyo on IRAA Resignations

subfiles.about: Reports the appointment of Sumitomo head Masatsune Ogura as Minister without Portfolio to coordinate wartime economic administration.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports the appointment of Masatsune Ogura, Director General of the Sumitomo interests, as Minister without Portfolio to direct national economic affairs. Ogura's appointment is intended to bridge government-business relations, curb bureaucratic inefficiencies, and resolve friction between the Finance Ministry, Commerce Ministry, and Planning Board. Ogura maintains close ties with Premier Konoye and Home Minister Hiranuma, with Hiranuma taking an active role in strengthening the Cabinet through consultations with financial and administrative figures. The press anticipates the formation of an inner ministerial council and a Supreme Economic Council to oversee wartime mobilization.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 495 from Tokyo on the Appointment of Masatsune Ogura

subfiles.about: Announces the appointments of Teijiro Toyoda as Minister of Commerce and Industry and Teiichi Suzuki as President of the Planning Board.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that newspaper extra editions announce the appointments of Vice Admiral Teijiro Toyoda as Minister of Commerce and Industry and Lieutenant General Teiichi Suzuki as President of the Cabinet Planning Board with the rank of Minister of State. Both appointees represent active-duty military leaders placed in charge of critical economic mobilization posts.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 506 from Tokyo on New Economic Appointments

subfiles.about: Analyzes the appointment of military officers to economic posts to accelerate wartime mobilization and eliminate bureaucratic conflict.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that the press describes the selection of Admiral Toyoda and General Suzuki as a blitz move to strengthen Japan's wartime Cabinet. The installation of active fighting service members signifies comprehensive Army-Navy cooperation to place the economy on a total war footing following the civilian tenures of Kobayashi and Hoshino. The press notes that the Commerce Ministry has effectively become a ministry of military production, with executive leadership now consolidated under the triumvirate of Konoye, Hiranuma, and Ogura. Peacetime industry circles express mild apprehension that resources will be further redirected toward armaments in preparation for a Pacific crisis.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 512 from Tokyo on Military Appointments to Economic Posts

subfiles.about: Summarizes the official announcement on the revised structure and administrative streamlining of the IRAA.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits an official press summary regarding the reorganized Imperial Rule Assistance Association. The reforms aim to clarify the association's original aims and establish closer connections with the government while simplifying administrative operations. Central headquarters will establish bureaus for general affairs, organization, and East Asia, alongside a training section. A vice president will manage daily operations and preside over a deliberative council advising the director general.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 502 from Tokyo on IRAA Reorganization Announcement

subfiles.about: Summarizes press commentary on Masatsune Ogura's appointment and coverage of Foreign Minister Matsuoka's diplomatic talks in Rome.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports editorial reactions to domestic and international developments. Japanese newspapers welcome Masatsune Ogura's appointment as an experienced financier capable of replacing bureaucratic management, though some note that one individual alone cannot resolve structural economic crises. Commentators praise Premier Konoye for shifting toward pragmatic governance. Meanwhile, the press covers Matsuoka's visit to Rome amidst the Yugoslavian crisis, viewing his discussions with the Italian government as enhancing his diplomatic prestige.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 503 from Tokyo on Press Reaction to Ogura and Matsuoka

subfiles.about: Reports confidential messages exchanged between Embassy Counselor Dooman and Fujii, representing Home Minister Baron Hiranuma.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that Counselor Dooman met twice with Mr. Fujii, a close confidant of Home Minister Baron Hiranuma. Fujii conveyed that Hiranuma had been alarmed by reports that the United States might take drastic action against Japan, appreciated the Embassy's explanations, and felt confident that restraints could be maintained in Japan to prevent conditions justifying U.S. security measures. Hiranuma invited further confidential exchanges through this channel. Grew recommends against seeking a direct interview with Hiranuma at present, citing the political risks for Hiranuma as his domestic influence expands.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 517 from Tokyo on Confidential Contacts with Baron Hiranuma

subfiles.about: Highlights for Under Secretary Welles a statement by Baron Hiranuma's confidant regarding the imposition of domestic restraints.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck submits a memorandum for Under Secretary of State Sumner Welles quoting Tokyo Telegram No. 517 of April 7. He draws attention to the statement made by Mr. Fujii on behalf of Baron Hiranuma expressing confidence that restraints could be imposed in Japan to prevent the United States from resorting to drastic measures. The memorandum is initialed as noted by Under Secretary Welles.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Stanley K. Hornbeck on Telegram No. 517 and Hiranuma's Assurance

subfiles.about: Summarizes Tokyo Telegram No. 517 regarding Baron Hiranuma's confidential assurances conveyed through his representative Fujii.
subfiles.summary: This State Department digest summarizes Telegram No. 517 of April 7, 1941. It records that Mr. Fujii conveyed a message from Baron Hiranuma, who was emerging as a dominant Cabinet figure. Hiranuma expressed concern over reports of potential immediate American countermeasures, but voiced confidence that steps could be taken in Japan to prevent situations necessitating drastic U.S. action.
subfiles.title: Digest of Tokyo Telegram No. 517 regarding Baron Hiranuma's Message

subfiles.about: Reports quiet dissemination of American views among Japanese leaders and proposes an interview with Prince Konoye before Matsuoka returns.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that the Embassy is quietly disseminating information and opinions among influential Japanese leaders to strengthen rational political elements, which is producing perceptible positive effects. He notes that the public atmosphere has shifted following the realization that the alliance with Germany failed to intimidate the United States. Grew plans to request an interview with Prince Konoye while he serves as acting Foreign Minister prior to Matsuoka's return. The ostensible purpose will be to review Admiral Nomura's conversations in Washington, while providing an opportunity to firmly present the American stance against Japan's southward advance.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 518 from Tokyo on Embassy Dissemination and Proposed Konoye Interview

subfiles.about: Provides guidance and talking points for Ambassador Grew's projected interview with Prince Konoye.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Hull provides guidance for Ambassador Grew's proposed interview with Prince Konoye. Grew is instructed to state that pending questions between Japan and the United States should be susceptible to adjustment without armed clash, but Japan must first manifest an attitude of conciliation. Hull emphasizes that Grew should stress that the United States is entirely convinced that Great Britain will not be defeated and is making all international calculations accordingly. Supporting departmental telegrams and instructions are cited for background material.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 223 to Tokyo providing Guidance for Konoye Meeting

subfiles.about: Reports Masatsune Ogura's formal investiture as Minister without Portfolio and statements by Konoye and Ogura regarding economic policies.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that Masatsune Ogura was formally invested as Minister without Portfolio to direct the national economy. Premier Konoye publicly acknowledged that neither he nor Home Minister Hiranuma possesses economic expertise, explaining that Ogura will coordinate economic ministries with the possible establishment of a brain trust or Supreme Economic Council. In press statements, Ogura expressed confidence in harmonizing economic policies and promised to cooperate with the Welfare Minister on labor matters. Justice Minister Yanagawa will concurrently assume the vice presidency of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 500 from Tokyo on Ogura's Investiture and Economic Plans

subfiles.about: Summarizes an address by Home Minister Baron Hiranuma warning of an imminent grave crisis in East Asia and British-American economic encirclement.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on Home Minister Baron Hiranuma's address to the Conference of Prefectural Governors. Hiranuma reviewed Japan's diplomatic achievements, including the basic treaty with China and Manchukuo and mediation of the Thailand-Indochina dispute, but warned of ongoing Chinese resistance and Anglo-American economic encirclement. He stated that a new grave crisis could break out in East Asia at any time, placing Japan before the greatest difficulties in its history, and called for steadfast dedication to establishing a new order.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 525 from Tokyo on Baron Hiranuma's Governors' Speech

subfiles.about: Reports editorial criticism of frequent Cabinet changes and discusses public expectations regarding Foreign Minister Matsuoka's European journey.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew summarizes newspaper editorials analyzing recent Cabinet shifts and Matsuoka's diplomatic mission. The Yomiuri criticizes the rapid turnover of economic ministers, noting that Japanese commerce ministers average only six months in office compared to five-year stability in Germany and continuity in China. Meanwhile, Kokumin evaluates Matsuoka's visits to Berlin, Rome, and Moscow as completely successful, noting his meetings with Molotov and Stalin. The press urges the nation to prepare for diplomatic developments following Matsuoka's return and anticipates how the United States will react.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 513 from Tokyo on Press Criticism and Matsuoka's Mission

subfiles.about: Reports Premier Konoye's address to prefectural governors and sharp press criticism of his vague explanations and lack of concrete leadership.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that Premier Konoye addressed the Conference of Prefectural Governors, urging cooperation in national restructuring and warning that the next two years would be critical for overcoming the national crisis. The vernacular press, including Nichi Nichi, Asahi, and Hochi, reacted with severe criticism, accusing Konoye of delivering vague philosophical rhetoric instead of concrete solutions after four years of war in China. Editorials demanded actionable plans for expanding industrial production, replenishing armaments, and rationalizing daily living conditions.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 524 (Sections 1–2) from Tokyo on Konoye's Governors' Address

subfiles.about: Records an internal departmental archival charge-out transaction for a loan of records.
subfiles.summary: This Department of State charge-out slip (Form DS-1038) records the temporary withdrawal of records from departmental archives. It indicates item 725.00 8-20 54 charged out on June 8, 1956. The form serves as an administrative tracking placeholder within the decimal filing system.
subfiles.title: Department of State Charge-Out Record (Form DS-1038)

subfiles.about: Reports confidential insights from an informant regarding Hiranuma's role, War Minister Tojo's restraint of Army radicals, and Matsuoka's mission.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew relays confidential intelligence from an influential Japanese informant who recently spoke with Baron Hiranuma. Hiranuma explained that he and Justice Minister Yanagawa entered the Cabinet to assist Prince Konoye in curbing radical Army elements, and that War Minister General Hideki Tojo is loyally cooperating by keeping military extremists in check. Tojo personally overcame Army opposition to install Yanagawa, an anti-German figure, as Minister of Justice. The informant noted that Matsuoka gained nothing tangible in Berlin, Rome, or Moscow, predicting that Japan may demonstrate a shift in international posture by May. Grew adds that newspaper articles by this informant arguing that Japan cannot expect U.S. cooperation under its present policies are attracting wide attention.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 536 from Tokyo on Cabinet Stability and Military Control

subfiles.about: Summarizes intelligence from Tokyo Telegram No. 536 concerning Hiranuma, Yanagawa, and War Minister Tojo's efforts to control Army radicals.
subfiles.summary: This State Department digest summarizes Telegram No. 536 of April 10, 1941. It outlines reporting from a Japanese informant who stated that Baron Hiranuma and General Yanagawa entered the Cabinet solely to support Premier Konoye in restraining radical elements in the Army and government. Hiranuma reported having the loyal cooperation of War Minister General Tojo, who was instrumental in overcoming extremist opposition to Yanagawa's appointment as Justice Minister.
subfiles.title: Digest of Tokyo Telegram No. 536 regarding Internal Cabinet Dynamics

subfiles.about: Summarizes Premier Konoye's formal press conference covering economic direction, China peace terms, South Seas policy, and U.S. relations.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew summarizes Premier Konoye's third formal press conference. Konoye stated that no further Cabinet changes or inner cabinet bodies are planned, confirming that economic management has been entrusted to Masatsune Ogura. In foreign affairs, Konoye maintained his policy of willingness to cooperate with Chungking if it abandons anti-Japanese policies, while continuing support for Wang Ching-wei and favoring an eventual Chiang-Wang merger. He disclaimed any intention to use armed force in the South Seas, asserted that the Tripartite Pact aims to prevent American entry into the European war, and expressed optimism that relations with the Soviet Union and United States could be peacefully resolved.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 543 / 534 from Tokyo on Premier Konoye's Press Conference

subfiles.about: Clarifies informal State Department comments on a confidential British text mentioned in Tokyo Telegram 534.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck writes a confidential letter to Ambassador Grew referencing Tokyo Telegram No. 534 of April 10. Hornbeck confirms that the Department received the British text in strict confidence through the American Ambassador in London and volunteered informal comments on one point, which the British Government subsequently modified. Hornbeck clarifies, however, that offering informal comment did not constitute formal diplomatic consultation with the British Government.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Joseph C. Grew regarding British Diplomatic Text

subfiles.about: Reports editorial support for Vice Foreign Minister Ohashi's appeal for courteous treatment of foreigners and the importance of foreign languages.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on a Nichi Nichi editorial discussing Vice Foreign Minister Chuichi Ohashi's speech to prefectural governors. Ohashi urged police and the public to treat foreign residents with greater consideration. The editorial strongly supports Ohashi's views, arguing that anti-foreign prejudice harms Japan's national honor and that foreign languages remain indispensable tools for diplomacy and international information.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 544 from Tokyo on Treatment of Foreigners and Languages

subfiles.about: Outlines the military career and background of Major General Sadaaki Kagesa, military adviser to the Nanking Government.
subfiles.summary: Lieutenant Colonel Harry I. T. Creswell submits a biographical report on Major General Sadaaki Kagesa. Born in Hiroshima Prefecture in 1893, Kagesa served in artillery, graduated from the Army Staff College, and held key posts in the Military Affairs Bureau and General Staff. He served as chief military delegate in peace negotiations with General Nobuyuki Abe and was appointed military adviser to Wang Ching-wei's National Government at Nanking in December 1940. Creswell evaluates Kagesa as one of the Army's foremost experts on Chinese affairs.
subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report No. 10,299: Major General Sadaaki Kagesa

subfiles.about: Details the service record and qualifications of Major General Shuitsu Tsuchihashi, appointed Military Attaché at Nanking.
subfiles.summary: Lieutenant Colonel Creswell outlines the career of Major General Shuitsu Tsuchihashi upon his appointment as Military Attaché to the Japanese Embassy in Nanking. Born in Saga Prefecture in 1891, Tsuchihashi graduated with honors from the Army Staff College, served in France, participated in League of Nations disarmament conferences in Geneva, and served as military attaché in France and Belgium before directing the Second Bureau of the General Staff. Creswell characterizes him as an able administrator and engaging conversationalist fluent in French and well versed in foreign affairs.
subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report No. 10,300: Major General Shuitsu Tsuchihashi

subfiles.about: Provides a career summary and personality assessment of Lieutenant General Shigeru Sawada, commander of Japanese forces in Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: Lieutenant Colonel Creswell submits a report on Lieutenant General Shigeru Sawada, newly appointed commander of Japanese forces in the Shanghai area. Born in Kochi Prefecture in 1887, Sawada served with the Siberian Expedition in Vladivostok, held military attaché postings in Greece, Poland, and Rumania, commanded a division in China, and served as Vice-Chief of the Army General Staff during the conclusion of the Tripartite Pact. Creswell notes that Sawada is considered an expert on Soviet Russia whose clear thinking and experience qualify him to navigate the complex international atmosphere in Shanghai.
subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report No. 10,301: Lieut. General Shigeru Sawada

subfiles.about: Reviews the military record and personality of Lieutenant General Shizuichi Tanaka, appointed Chief of the Military Police.
subfiles.summary: Lieutenant Colonel Creswell outlines the career of Lieutenant General Shizuichi Tanaka on his second appointment as Chief of the Military Police (Kempeitai). Born in Hyogo Prefecture in 1887, Tanaka served as assistant military attaché in England, military attaché in Mexico and Washington, and head of the British Section of the General Staff, as well as holding field commands in Shanghai and Manchuria. Creswell describes Tanaka as speaking English and Spanish, possessing a congenial disposition, and retaining pleasant recollections of his service in the United States.
subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report No. 10,302: Lieut. General Shizuichi Tanaka

subfiles.about: Details the career and diplomatic significance of Lieutenant General Hiroshi Oshima's reappointment as Ambassador to Germany.
subfiles.summary: Lieutenant Colonel Creswell reviews the career of Lieutenant General Hiroshi Oshima following his reappointment as Ambassador to Germany in December 1940. Born in Tokyo in 1886, Oshima served extensively in Berlin as military attaché and ambassador, playing a central role in negotiating the Anti-Comintern Pact before resigning following the 1939 German-Soviet pact. Creswell reports that Oshima speaks German well, maintains close ties with German officials, and that his return to Berlin is viewed as a political vindication of his advocacy for the Tripartite Alliance.
subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report No. 10,303: Lieut. General Hiroshi Oshima

subfiles.about: Summarizes the military record of Lieutenant General Kisaburo Hamamoto, appointed Commander of the Northern Army District.
subfiles.summary: Lieutenant Colonel Creswell reports on the routine appointment of Lieutenant General Kisaburo Hamamoto as Commander of the Northern Army District at Sapporo, Hokkaido. Born in Kyoto in 1885, Hamamoto held staff and instructional posts at the Infantry School and Military Academy, commanded an infantry regiment during the 1931 Manchurian Incident, served as chief of staff of the 7th Division, and led combat units in South China. Hamamoto is well regarded throughout the Army as an educator and decorated combat leader awarded the Order of the Golden Kite.
subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report No. 10,304: Lieut. General Kisaburo Hamamoto

subfiles.about: Outlines the military service and foreign assignments of Lieutenant General Masaharu Homma, appointed Commander of the Taiwan Army.
subfiles.summary: Lieutenant Colonel Creswell reports on the career of Lieutenant General Masaharu Homma upon his appointment to command the Taiwan Army. Born in Niigata Prefecture in 1887, Homma graduated with honors from the Army Staff College, served as a military observer with British forces during World War I, and completed resident officer assignments in England and India. He served as aide-de-camp to Prince Chichibu, military attaché in London, head of the War Department Press Section, and director of the Second Bureau (G-2) of the General Staff before commanding divisions in North and Central China.
subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report No. 10,305: Lieut. General Masaharu Homma
